header:
Date: 2026-12-18
Start: 15:00 UTC
Duration: 45 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Ethan Park (Redwood SE), Sarah Ortiz (Lumen - Head of Security), Raj Patel (Lumen - Platform Eng), Diane Wu (Lumen - PM)
summary: Redwood team walked Lumen Payments through data handling and retention controls available via the API, Console, and Redwood Optimize. Focus on logging redaction, PII scrubbing, request storage toggles, and KMS integrations. Customer confirmed security/regulatory constraints and interest in a short Dedicated pilot and a POC benchmark. Next steps: share SOC2/KMS docs, redaction demo artifacts, and schedule pilot benchmarking.
transcript:
[00:00] Maya Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, we really appreciate the time. Today we'll demo our data retention and PII controls across the API, Console and Redwood Optimize. Ethan will drive the technical side.
[00:08] Ethan Park: Hi all, hi Sarah, Raj, Diane. I'll share my screen in a sec, but quick agenda: logging redaction, request storage toggles, how request/response payloads can be excluded from retention, KMS/HSM encryption options, and a quick Optimize walkthrough for detection and alerting on quality regressions tied to retained prompts.
[00:22] Sarah Ortiz: Great. For context, Lumen has strict data residency and PCI-adjacent controls; we need to ensure no cardholder data is stored, and any PII is either redacted at ingestion or auto-scrubbed. Also SSO and audit logs are required.
[00:35] Ethan Park: Totally, that's the right place to start. We're assuming you're using Redwood API for hosted inference today?
[00:42] Raj Patel: We're evaluating hosted vs Dedicated. Security would prefer dedicated or private, but we need to see the retention toggles and how easy it is to opt out of request storage for certain endpoints.
[00:52] Maya Chen: Yep and that's common; we typically show both the Console flow and the API flag based approach.
[00:58] Ethan Park: (shares screen) Alright, Console first. Here is the project settings page, under Data & Retention. You can see toggles: "Store requests" (on/off), "Automatic PII Redaction" (off/on), and retention window dropdowns (1 day, 7 days, 30 days, custom).
[01:18] Raj Patel: Is that tenant-level or route-level? I don't want a global off for everything.
[01:24] Ethan Park: Good question — we support route-level overrides. You can set defaults at the project level and then per-route overrides in the API route config. So you can keep storage on for analytics routes and disable for payment-intent routes.
[01:36] Diane Wu: How does Automatic PII Redaction work? Is it regex-based or ML-based?
[01:41] Ethan Park: It's a hybrid. We run a light-weight ML classifier that first identifies PHI/PII candidates, then apply configurable redaction rules (regex, token masking, custom entity lists). There's a preview mode in Console so you can inspect sample requests with redactions applied before enabling wide rollouts.
[01:58] Sarah Ortiz: Can we add our own sensitive token patterns — like internal account IDs that aren't standard SSNs?
[02:04] Ethan Park: Absolutely — you can upload custom patterns or a snippet list in the project settings. Those patterns are evaluated server-side during ingestion. You can also request offline scanning for historical data.
[02:15] Maya Chen: Also note we store redaction rules in your control plane and you can opt to encrypt those via your KMS.
[02:23] Raj Patel: Speaking of encryption, what's the KMS story? We use AWS KMS and a vault.
[02:28] Ethan Park: We support customer-managed keys (CMK) via AWS KMS, Azure Key Vault, and HashiCorp Vault. For Private deployments you can use an HSM. Keys are used to encrypt at rest for request payloads that are marked as "stored"; for ephemeral/no-store requests there's nothing written.
[02:43] Sarah Ortiz: And audit logs for who changed retention rules and redaction configs?
[02:48] Ethan Park: Yes, Console's admin audit logs capture config changes, who made them, and we export via S3 or syslog. For Dedicated we also provide a more detailed audit package.
[02:58] Diane Wu: Back to the API — how do we opt out at the request level?
[03:02] Ethan Park: On the API side there's a header flag: X-Redwood-Store-Requests: true/false. If false, the payload is not persisted. There's also X-Redwood-Redact: strict|relaxed|none to apply server-side redaction policies on a per-request basis.
[03:18] Raj Patel: What's the guarantee — eventual, immediate? If a request arrives with store=false, is there any chance we still log it for debugging?
[03:25] Ethan Park: By default, no. If store=false, we don't persist the request body. There is a separate debug mode that can be turned on by an admin; when enabled, debug logs can be captured but are also gated by a retention window and require admin approval. We can also sign a contractual clause for not enabling debug logs for your tenant in Hosted mode if that's required.
[03:42] Sarah Ortiz: Is there any PII in the model embeddings or is that separate?
[03:48] Ethan Park: Embeddings can contain latent PII; we treat them like other artifacts. You can choose to not store embeddings, or store with masking / KMS encryption. There's an Optimize setting that can flag unusual embedding similarity patterns that look like repeated PHI and alert.
[04:03] Maya Chen: Quick demo — Ethan, show the redaction preview on a sample payment payload.
[04:08] Ethan Park: Sure — loading sample. (typing) Here's a request with name, email, last4 of the card, and internal account ID. Preview mode shows email -> ****@*****.com, name partial redaction, and last4 masked to XX34. The internal account ID matched a custom pattern so it's replaced with [REDACTED-ACCT].
[04:28] Raj Patel: Nice. Is that done client-side or server-side?
[04:31] Ethan Park: Server-side during ingestion before any persistence. The preview runs on the same pipeline but in a dry-run mode.
[04:37] Diane Wu: What about export — if we export logs for internal analytics, does redaction persist in exported data?
[04:42] Ethan Park: Exports respect the active retention and redaction rules. You can export raw (only if retention policy allowed and you have keys) or export redacted copies. There's an option to watermark exported datasets to indicate redaction.
[04:54] Sarah Ortiz: For compliance we need retention windows enforced automatically. Can we set policy that deletes after 7 days and that is non-reversible?
[05:01] Ethan Park: Yes, we have immutable retention policies. For Hosted we provide deletion workflows and a retention engine that will permanently purge data. For Dedicated/Private we give you admin controls with SLA and can support retention enforcement and periodic attestations.
[05:13] Maya Chen: Many customers in payments choose Dedicated for the stronger contractual guarantees and on-prem key control. That said, hosted with CMK and no-store flags works for some.
[05:23] Raj Patel: Another question — does Redwood keep any system logs that might leak request data (like full request traces)?
[05:29] Ethan Park: System logs are scrubbed. We separate tracing data from payloads. Trace IDs are stored but payloads are not attached unless you have debugging enabled. We also have an internal process for access controls, and access is audited.
[05:41] Diane Wu: Can we bring our own redaction engine? We'd prefer to run certain classifiers internally.
[05:46] Ethan Park: For Private deployments yes. For Hosted Dedicated we can integrate your webhook or allow a pre-ingest callback to your endpoint for redaction decisions — latency sensitive but possible. For strict regulatory requirements we recommend Private.
[05:58] Sarah Ortiz: What's the SLA on deletion if we request a purge?
[06:02] Ethan Park: For Hosted it's typically 72 hours to full purge depending on retention tier. For Dedicated we can contractually agree on a shorter window, like 24 hours, as part of the reserved capacity contract.
[06:12] Maya Chen: I'll call out a couple product notes: We also have a policy engine in Optimize that can auto-scan prompts for sensitive patterns and create alerts or auto-redact. It can run batch jobs if you want to scan historical logs.
[06:25] Raj Patel: That sounds useful for drift detection too.
[06:28] Ethan Park: Exactly — Optimize ties quality regressions to input prompt sets and can notify you if a new prompt population increases PII leakage.
[06:35] (short pause, typing)
[06:39] Sarah Ortiz: Two more compliance bits: SSO provisioning and RBAC roles — we need to map admin roles to our internal IDs.
[06:45] Ethan Park: We support SAML/SSO, SCIM provisioning, and fine-grained RBAC. We can sync groups and map to roles in Console.
[06:52] Diane Wu: If we go Dedicated, how do rollouts and model upgrades work? We don't want a hidden model change to change outputs and inadvertently capture PII differently.
[07:00] Ethan Park: We support pinned model versions and rollout policies — canarying, A/B, and automatic fallback. Any model change is logged in the audit trail. Optimize also lets you pin evaluation sets to detect regressions pre-rollout.
[07:12] Raj Patel: For the pilot, we'd like to test a small flow with redaction rules and the store=false header and run benchmarks for latency impact.
[07:19] Maya Chen: Great — that's standard. For the POC we can provide a small Dedicated pool for a month or a hosted isolated tenant with contractual no-debug. We'll include sample configs and a short checklist.
[07:29] Ethan Park: I'll prepare a benchmark checklist: sample payloads, PII patterns, latency targets, retention validation steps.
[07:36] Diane Wu: Any limitations on throughput when redaction is enabled?
[07:39] Ethan Park: There's a slight CPU cost at ingest for ML-based redaction; on average it's <5% latency increase for typical payloads. For high-throughput pipelines we recommend enabling the lightweight regex-first mode or using Dedicated with autoscaling pools.
[07:55] Sarah Ortiz: Can we get an architecture diagram and a short data flow that shows exactly where data is redacted, encrypted, and stored?
[08:01] Maya Chen: Yes — we'll send an architecture diagram and the redaction flow chart.
[08:06] Raj Patel: One last question — retention of derived artifacts like KV cache. If we do a private deployment, is the KV cache persisted?
[08:14] Ethan Park: KV cache is ephemeral by design; it's per-session and not persisted beyond session unless you explicitly enable session replay or persistent conversation storage. Those are governed by the same retention rules.
[08:25] Maya Chen: Ok let's recap quick.
[08:27] Maya Chen: Action items: Ethan will provide redaction demo artifacts and the recording; Raj will share sample payloads; Maya will send SOC2 and KMS docs and pilot pricing.
[08:38] Raj Patel: Sounds good.
[08:40] Diane Wu: Thanks everyone.
[08:42] Sarah Ortiz: Thanks — we'll review and aim to get payloads to you by Monday.
[08:46] Ethan Park: Thank you all, we'll follow up with the deck and the Checklist.
[08:50] Maya Chen: End meeting.

Note: transcription has minor mis-hearings; some technical terms displayed as separate letters (e.g., S-A-M-L) in parts.
